papers.title: TRACER: Twin-contrastive learning for fine-grained and rare spatial domain identification in spatial transcriptomics.
papers.summary: TRACER is a new computational method that uses a twin-contrastive learning approach to analyze spatial transcriptomics data. It is specifically designed to identify spatial domains—regions with distinct gene expression patterns—with a focus on detecting fine-grained and rare domains that other methods might miss. This could improve the ability to map subtle or small tissue regions based on their molecular signatures.
papers.why: This tool could help identify rare or fine-grained spatial domains such as specific interneuron subtypes or perineuronal net-associated regions within spatial transcriptomics datasets of brain tissue.
papers.figure: A figure showing benchmark comparisons of TRACER against other spatial domain identification methods on tissue sections with known fine-grained or rare domains, ideally including brain tissue examples.

papers.title: ARCADE disentangles cell abundance from continuous transcriptional state in spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: ARCADE is a computational method designed to separate two things that are often tangled together in spatial transcriptomics data: how many cells are present in a region and what continuous transcriptional state those cells are in. By disentangling cell abundance from gene expression state, it aims to give a clearer, more accurate picture of tissue composition and cell activity across space. This could improve the reliability of spatial transcriptomics analyses, particularly in tissues with complex or gradient-like cell states.
papers.why: This tool could help more accurately map interneuron subtypes and their transcriptional states within perineuronal net-associated microenvironments in spatial transcriptomics datasets, improving disentanglement of cell density effects from true state changes relevant to mitophagy/autophagy signaling.

papers.title: Spatialsnake: a flexible workflow for spatial transcriptomics analysis across platforms
papers.summary: Spatialsnake is a computational workflow designed to analyze spatial transcriptomics data generated from multiple different platforms in a unified way. It likely standardizes preprocessing, quality control, and downstream analysis steps so that researchers can compare or combine datasets from different spatial technologies. The tool aims to make spatial transcriptomics analysis more flexible, reproducible, and accessible across experimental setups.
papers.why: A flexible cross-platform workflow could be directly applied to analyze spatial transcriptomics data from brain tissue to map interneuron subtypes and perineuronal net-associated gene expression relevant to this PhD project.

papers.title: CellMarker 3.0: an updated resource of manually curated and computationally predicted cell markers in human/mouse and interactive web tools for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics analysis.
papers.summary: CellMarker 3.0 is an updated database that catalogs cell type marker genes for humans and mice, combining manually curated literature data with computationally predicted markers. It provides interactive web-based tools designed to help researchers annotate cell types in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics datasets. The resource aims to streamline the process of matching gene expression signatures to known cell identities across many tissue and cell types.
papers.why: This database could help with annotating interneuron subtypes and other neuronal/glial populations in spatial transcriptomics data, supporting cell-type identification in brain tissue analyses relevant to the mitophagy and perineuronal net research.

papers.title: SpaceBlocks: an expert-supervised workflow for cohort-level spatial transcriptomics analysis
papers.summary: SpaceBlocks is a new computational workflow designed to analyze spatial transcriptomics data across multiple samples or patient cohorts at once. It incorporates expert human supervision into the analysis pipeline, likely to improve annotation accuracy or quality control compared to fully automated methods. The tool aims to streamline large-scale spatial transcriptomics studies by standardizing workflows across cohorts.
papers.why: This workflow could help structure cohort-level spatial transcriptomics analysis of interneuron and perineuronal net markers across multiple brain samples, improving reproducibility in the PhD project's spatial data pipeline.

papers.title: Ultrasound-Guided Mobilization of Dual Autophagic Cleaning Crew by Exosomal Rapamycin Ameliorates the Progression of Parkinsonism.
papers.summary: This paper describes a therapy for Parkinson's disease using exosomes (tiny cell-derived vesicles) loaded with rapamycin, a drug known to boost autophagy. The exosomes are guided to the brain using focused ultrasound, which helps them cross the blood-brain barrier and reach affected tissue. The treatment aims to activate autophagy and mitophagy pathways to clear toxic protein aggregates and damaged mitochondria, slowing disease progression in a Parkinsonism model.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it targets autophagy and mitophagy modulation in neurons using a novel delivery method, offering therapeutic context and potential mechanistic insights for neuronal clearance pathways central to the PhD project.

papers.title: Enhancing cell type deconvolution in spatial transcriptomics through incorporating multiple reference panels.
papers.summary: This paper addresses a technical challenge in spatial transcriptomics: accurately estimating which cell types are present at each spatial location (deconvolution). The authors propose a method that combines information from multiple reference datasets, rather than relying on just one, to improve accuracy. This multi-reference approach aims to reduce bias and improve robustness when reference panels differ in cell type composition or quality.
papers.why: Accurate cell type deconvolution is essential for correctly mapping interneuron subtypes and their spatial relationship to perineuronal nets in spatial transcriptomics datasets used in this project.

papers.title: Probabilistic uncertainty in virtual spatial transcriptomics from histology is largely redundant with the predicted mean
papers.summary: This paper examines models that predict spatial gene expression patterns directly from histology images, a technique known as virtual spatial transcriptomics. It investigates whether the uncertainty estimates these models provide (how confident they are in their predictions) actually add new information beyond just the predicted average values. The findings suggest that in most cases, the uncertainty measure doesn't offer much extra insight and largely mirrors the predicted mean itself.
papers.why: Since this PhD project relies on spatial transcriptomics to study interneurons and perineuronal nets, understanding whether AI-predicted uncertainty in virtual transcriptomics is trustworthy or redundant is critical for correctly interpreting such data when histology-based prediction methods are used as a substitute or complement to direct spatial measurements.
